judge_panel.reason: The paper only compares the full two-stage XCT-SAM against Conv-LoRA-SAM fine-tuned directly on XCT data ('Following the direct synthetic-XCT adaptation setting of [18], we fine-tune this baseline on GAN-generated XCT images without the intermediate alloy-microstructure [34] adaptation stage'), with no epoch-matched controls, no alternative intermediate domain ablations, no Stage-I-only baseline, and no analysis ruling out that longer training rather than sequential adaptation explains the gain.

The paper compares sequential adaptation only against direct Conv-LoRA fine-tuning: "we fine-tune this baseline on GAN-generated XCT images without the intermediate alloy-microstructure [34] adaptation stage used in XCT-SAM," while XCT-SAM itself uses extra training stages ("In Stage 1... up to 15 epochs... In Stage 2... an additional 20 epochs"). No epoch-matched control, Stage-I-only result, or alternative intermediate-domain ablation is reported.

The paper does not provide an explicit epoch-matched control for the direct adaptation baseline, nor does it present ablations for alternative intermediate domains or Stage-I-only controls; it only notes that baselines 'are optimized using the same XCT training data'.

The reviewer is correct; the paper explicitly admits in Section IV.A that 'Since manually annotated ground-truth defect masks are not publicly available, we generate threshold-derived binary reference masks', confirming that NIST evaluations rely on rule-based masks rather than human annotations.

Section III.A relies entirely on citation [18] to justify independent binary models, stating 'We adopt this multi-model formulation because prior work reported that joint multi-class training under extreme imbalance leads to reduced generalization performance', with no joint-multiclass baseline evaluated on the authors' own data.

judge_panel.reason: The paper presents per-test comparisons in Fig. 5 with error bars (±1 std) that visibly overlap between models on several test sets, yet Sec. IV.E describes differences as clear improvements (e.g., 'outperforming the next best method, Conv-LoRA-SAM, by a substantial margin') without reporting any statistical significance tests.

The paper does not report significance testing, and Fig. 5 says the error bars are "±1 std." However, the main quantitative claim is framed at the aggregate level—"XCT-SAM achieves the best IoU and Dice performance across the three evaluation settings"—rather than as explicit per-test significance claims, so the reviewer’s objection is only partially supported.
